Although the story is told from Ilse's limited third-person point of view, it convincingly portrays a difficult, prickly character while also accurately conveying the contrasting perspective of her son, Jonas. Ilse can be seen as cold and unappealing in how she treats her son—ignoring his letters, refusing to look at him, and shutting down conversation—yet the writer makes her mindset entirely believable by grounding it in grief for Henning, fear of change, and a deep sense of duty to her daily routine. At the same time, Jonas’s pragmatic and concerned perspective (recognizing that the aging ferry cannot last forever and wanting to care for his mother) comes through clearly and empathetically through his dialogue and body language, creating two distinct, three-dimensional viewpoints in a very short space.
